title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
text:
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
- Published
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US, AP reports.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms ensure it had a competitive edge.
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

title: STAT+: RFK Jr. spills his calendar into public, but leaves much to the imagination
summary: A partially redacted calendar showing health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s activities was made public on Tuesday.
text:
WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar.
While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.”
In June, after a New York Times report referred to him as disengaged with the job, Kennedy said on social media that his calendar was publicly available, though no such calendar had been made available for the media or the public before Tuesday. A number of Freedom of Information Act requests filed by STAT reporters had previously gone unanswered and even unacknowledged and do not appear to be included in the Tuesday release.
Much of the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026, is redacted, including some private calls taken by the secretary. One of his closest aides at the agency, Stefanie Spear, appears to be listed only once in the calendar. References to other notable meetings are not redacted, including one that would ultimately lead to the ouster of a short-lived director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez.

title: What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
summary: Some California homeowners have spent thousands making their homes safer from wildfires. Yet all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills. Should they be getting a bigger break?
text:
What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
As a homeowner in rural Northern California, I've lost a lot of sleep worrying about fires. It's not just that big, destructive ones are becoming more common. It's that finding affordable and reliable home insurance has become a nightmare. Without it, the most valuable asset I own could literally go up in smoke. And we've been stuck in a broken insurance market, hoping someone or something can fix it.
Which is why I was so gripped by Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi's recent two-part series on our Planet Money podcast. And it's left me thinking about the economics of making our communities safer. Insurers are spending money to figure out how to keep houses from burning down. Yet some California homeowners tell him they're investing heavily to make their homes and communities safer, and all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills.
In the first episode, Alexi goes to a destruction lab in South Carolina where researchers use "crash-test dummies for houses" — the type of wonderful turn of phrase that we love Alexi for — to figure out what actually works to help homes survive climate disasters. They literally light mock houses on fire and subject them to hail and hurricane-force winds to see what happens to them.
Who pays for this lab? Some of the world's biggest insurance companies. They want to know how risky homes are to insure and which building designs will limit damage and shrink the payouts they have to make if disasters strike. It's a pretty wild way to tackle an increasingly urgent question: can we make homes that can better withstand fires and other disasters?
Alexi touches on this in the pod, but insurers have been running experiments like these for more than a century. Back in the early 20th century, scientists at an insurer-funded organization called Underwriters Laboratories tested out new kinds of electrical wiring and consumer appliances to try to reduce the risk of costly fires and electrical accidents. An outfit called the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety does something similar for cars, using crash tests to push for safer auto designs.
Fighting moral hazard in fire country
The insurance industry is way more interesting than most people give it credit for. Part of the magic is obvious. It can insulate us from financial devastation. But there can also be magic in how insurers figure out how big risks really are and what it takes to reduce them. That destruction lab in South Carolina is an amazing example of that.
But Alexi's reporting has me wondering whether insurers could do more to reduce risk. It has to do with this weird thing about insurance. If someone else picks up the tab when something goes wrong, you may have less reason to do everything you can to make sure that it doesn't go wrong in the first place. Economists call this "moral hazard." It's the idea that insurance can reduce incentives to mitigate risk.

title: When Disaster Strikes, Medicaid Work Rules Add Barriers for Potential Enrollees
summary: Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work requirements create barriers for those trying to recover from natural disasters.
text:
PO‘IPŪ, Hawai‘i — A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool’s concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean.
On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to about 1,800 nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a sharp decline in visitors. The number of Medicaid applications submitted by island residents jumped by about 50% in the following month, according to the Hawaiʻi Department of Human Services.
In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January.
In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies on a federal law that allows the president to issue a disaster or emergency declaration and authorizes federal assistance, but any declaration can take months or may not come at all.
Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it’s unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn’t offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees.
Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel’s hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn’t hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities.
Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to delay enforcing the work requirements until next July, but states are still expected to implement eligibility checks by Jan. 1.

title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
summary: Here is what you need to know about the payment that millions will receive from January.
text:
Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
- Published
Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.
Here's what you need to know about the payment.
How much is it?
For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.
A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.
Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.
Will I get the payment? And how can I check?
Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.
As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in, external. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.
If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.
Will I get it if I live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland?
The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.
The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes.
The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.

If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account.
Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.
The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.
Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.
However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.
Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments.

title: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about Sanofi buying Insmed, Roche touting its breast cancer pill, and more
summary: Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs
text:
Hello there from STAT’s London bureau, with reporter Andrew Joseph here filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for a few days. It may be a holiday week stateside, but the news, at least for now, has yet to let up. So grab your choice cup of stimulation and settle in. …
Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs, STAT tells us. The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its blockbuster inflammatory drug Dupixent. Sanofi has been upfront that it was searching for takeover targets with late-stage or clinical assets, and with the deal, it will get New Jersey-based Insmed’s two lung disease drugs.
Roche touted the blockbuster potential of a new breast cancer pill after winning two U.S. regulatory approvals within a week, Bloomberg shares. The new medicine, called Wilserdly, is central to the drugmaker’s plan to regain its footing in the fast-growing cancer market. The company is positioning the pill to replace decades-old hormone therapies that are taken for years in an effort to reduce the risk the cancer will return. Estimates from analysts placing its peak annual sales potential at $9 billion are roughly in line with its own expectations, the Swiss drugmaker said.

title: They attended Trump's meme coin dinner. It didn't go well
summary: Trump's meme coin dinners have sparked intense controversy. These two guests attended his latest on Sunday — and agreed to provide NPR inside access.
text:
They attended Trump's meme coin dinner. It didn't go well
Headed to what some have called "the most exclusive dinner in the world," hosted by President Trump, crypto investor Morten Christensen and his young sister Gabriëlle Felen had butterflies in their stomachs.
The dinner on Sunday, Nov. 22, was meant to reward the top holders of the president's meme coin — a type of crypto currency that Trump had launched just days before his inauguration.
"I'm excited!," said Christensen. "It's always nice to dress up for an event. My sister looks amazing!"
Christensen — the founder of a crypto website called Airdrop Alert — is a veteran trader who got the crypto bug as far back as 2013. He has attended each of the previous two events Trump has held for the top holders of his meme coin.
For him it was just a chance to get a glimpse of the president. Christensen said that he's not political — and always advises others to "never buy a political meme coin ever."
The events have been intensely controversial. Anti-corruption activists have said they pose enormous conflicts of interest concerns, effectively rewarding those who buy the most coins with access to the president. Top buyers get the closest access.
Christensen was unsure if he would attend this latest dinner. But a sharp drop in the value of Trump's meme coin — from a peak of over $70 in January 2025 to now less than a dollar — had sharply reduced the cost of qualifying as a top holder, which provides access to the dinner.
And, above all, it was a chance to bring his sister Felen for the ride.
On Sunday night, Christensen and Felen agreed to provide NPR with voice memos through an event that turned out to be something they likely won't forget.
Disappointments begin early in the evening
Their butterflies started in the Uber ride to the Trump National Golf Club in Potomac Falls, Virginia. They wanted to head there early. By the time they cleared security, the large room was still filling in.
One of the first things Felen — a recent college graduate — saw was the gift boxes: They contained perfumes, a watch — and a small golden statue of President Trump.
"Pretty nice, pretty nice," said an excited Felen.
The excitement was short-lived.
Christensen bought enough meme coins to qualify as a VIP guest — but when he tried to access the area reserved for the top guests he was denied entry. He was told his name was not on the list.
"Apparently I got removed from the VIP list and I don't know," Christensen said, adding he had even gotten email confirmation.
"But I'm still at the event, so it's all good. It's just a shame."
Many guests appeared to be foreign
Perhaps the most controversial aspect of Trump's meme coin dinners is that many of the top buyers of the meme coin were believed to have been foreign citizens — raising concerns they could be trying to court influence with the president.

title: As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
summary: Since 2025, at least four states have enacted laws restricting medical malpractice lawsuits. Patient advocates warn that the laws impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth and often pass with little attention.
text:
As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
When Anyssa Zancanella’s water broke during a family vacation near Salt Lake City, she expected better care there than she could get back home in rural Rock Springs, Wyoming, where many patients are flown out for emergency treatment.
Instead, a crisis unfolded. Staff kept raising her doses of Pitocin, a drug that strengthens contractions, while the fetal monitor recorded mounting distress: The baby wasn’t getting enough oxygen. It took nearly 12 hours for the then-19-year-old to get an emergency cesarean section after the monitor showed signs of fetal distress, according to court records.
Azaylee, now 7, was born with brain damage, likely from a reduced supply of oxygen and blood flow during delivery, causing cognitive disabilities, according to her family’s complaint. Last year, a judge found Steward Health Care, a Dallas-based for-profit health system that owned the West Valley City, Utah, hospital at the time, liable for gross medical negligence — and awarded the family $951 million. Steward Health Care did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
Medical malpractice lawsuits against OB-GYNs are common in the U.S. healthcare system — childbirth can carry high risk and serious consequences. As a result, medical malpractice insurance costs for OB-GYNs are higher than for other specialties. Hospital administrators repeatedly cite the costs of those lawsuits and medical liability premiums as a reason to close their labor and delivery units. So, in recent years, state lawmakers began turning to what they say is a solution: tougher limits on malpractice lawsuits.
Since 2025, at least four states, including Oklahoma, have enacted restrictions on medical malpractice suits. Utah added protections shielding physicians’ personal assets. New Mexico capped punitive damages, which punish wrongdoing beyond financial losses, and raised the standard of proof, requiring “clear and convincing” evidence for punitive damages. And Arkansas shortened the window a patient can file those suits after delivery.
The laws often pass with little fanfare, and patient advocates warn they impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth, many of whom don’t realize for years that they’ve been survivors of medical malpractice.
“You really don’t know what you need to be looking for. You just know that you’re hurting,” said Deirdre Dickson-Gilbert, founder and national director of the National Medical Malpractice Advocacy Association. “And by the time you find out, the statutes of limitation are over with.”
Other critics say the actions ignore alternative ways to retain obstetricians, such as addressing abortion bans, which several states pursued in this month’s midterm elections.

title: For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
summary: Some who have worked to promote diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley say Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO sends a message that all that matters is money.
text:
For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day.
On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.
It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.
In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.
"I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.
To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.
"But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."
To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.
The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.
Spy intrigue overshadows workplace transgressions
Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.
"It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.
After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.
That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.
"Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.
The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."
Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.
"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia

title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
text:
US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
- Published
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down more than 7% in early afternoon trading, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's return was announced.

title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia as CEO after scandal
summary: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO was followed by to a surge in the tech company's stock -- and the stock market.
text:
Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia as CEO after scandal
Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO was followed by to a surge in the tech company's stock — and the stock market.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
Nvidia's stock rose more than 30% yesterday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:
In fact, the entire stock market rallied. The indexes had already been pointing upward before the news and then soared. Nvidia's stock alone increased in value by just under $1 trillion.
MARTIN: Our colleague, Ricky Mulvey, with The Indicator From Planet Money, our daily economic podcast, is with us now to tell us more. Good morning, Ricky.
RICKY MULVEY, BYLINE: Good morning.
MARTIN: So why are investors so happy about Jensen Huang coming back?
MULVEY: Well, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. Investors were happy to put the scandals aside and said that Jensen Huang is a good chunk of the company's value. And that boost, about $950 billion of market cap, is the biggest one-day gain for a single company ever. And for context, that's in the ballpark of all of Walmart's stock, who, as you may know, is the largest private sector employer in the United States.
MARTIN: So as you've said, and you're not the only person to say this, that Jensen Huang is Nvidia, how does that translate into the broader market?
MULVEY: Well, Jensen is one of the chief storytellers and central bankers in the AI economy. So much of the stock market now is a bet on artificial intelligence, and Jensen Huang has persuasively told investors why this bet is a good one, saying AI will create high-paying jobs and fundamentally change the economy.

title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
summary: There were legitimate fears before Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia - and his return won't fix it
text:
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
- Published
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.
Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.
President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.
In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.
They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

title: Menopause hormone therapy med popularity increases 141% compared to previous years
summary: In June 2026, 4.9M menopause hormone therapy medications were dispensed to cisgender women in the U.S. between the ages of 40 and 74.
text:
Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Good morning. We’ve got a “Beaver Moon” today. And, of course, there’s Thanksgiving later this week. Here’s a poem for both and neither.
An FDA milestone for limb girdle muscular dystrophy
Yesterday the FDA approved the first drug to treat limb girdle muscular dystrophy, a broad collection of progressive muscle conditions that has long received scant attention from physicians and drug developers. The drug, developed by BridgeBio, is specifically approved for patients with a subtype of the disease that the company estimates affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe.
“I’m pretty excited about it,” Nicholas Johnson, an LGMD specialist at Virginia Commonwealth University, told STAT’s Jason Mast. “It does appear that they had actually surprisingly robust effects on clinical outcome measures… and it also looks like it’s incredibly safe, so that’s a win-win.” Read more on the approval.
Why Barbara Kingsolver stopped signing books
The Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Barbara Kingsolver was learning to play hand drums when her fingers started curling in on themselves. She was diagnosed with a genetic condition called Dupuytren contracture, in which the tissue of a person’s palm thickens and tightens, pulling on the fingers.
While the condition is genetic, doctors believe that the gene needs to be turned on in some way — either through age or perhaps a trauma. The drums may have been Kingsolver’s trigger, according to her hand surgeon at the University of Virginia, Bobby Chhabra.
The condition quickly began to impact her work. As a sort of celebrity author, Kingsolver’s book signings are no small feat. “The way I have to do it is sign 60,000 books — that’s an actual figure,” Kingsolver said at a media briefing with UVA on Monday. “It involves hours every day of clenching a pen. And every time I did that, I’d have to go in for another surgery.”
Kingsolver has stopped signing books en masse, but she bristles when people recommend speech-to-text technology for her writing. “This is the way I write, and I need hands,” she said. “As long as I’ve got them, and as long as I can keep them, I’m going to keep writing books.”
4.9 million
In June 2026, that’s how many menopause hormone therapy medications were dispensed to cisgender women in the U.S. between the ages of 40 and 74. It’s a major increase — 141% — from the roughly 2.1 million meds dispensed monthly between July 2023 and February 2024. That’s according to an analysis of national data published last week in JAMA.
The study found that dispensing rose before and after the FDA’s removal of the black box warning in November 2025. Menopause and its precursor, perimenopause, received a flood of attention in those years, reflected in a still-booming business.

text:

STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:
Jeffrey Sonnenfeld has been listening with us. He's a professor of leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. He also founded the nonprofit Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which focuses on CEOs and corporate governance. Dr. Sonnenfeld, good morning.
JEFFREY SONNENFELD: Good morning, Steve. Good to hear from you.
INSKEEP: What do you make of the board's judgment after they got a suggestion from the U.S. government that Jensen Huang was candid after all?
SONNENFELD: This is amazing. This is a new high - well, low watermark in American business history. This is a very inglorious moment. I can't think of a worse board. I've been studying corporate boards and board governance for - well, as you know, for, well, about 50 years. I've never seen anything this bad. This is worse than Enron or WorldCom. It's a complete abdication of their responsibilities.
INSKEEP: Now, when you say the board is a bad board, you mean that the people on it were not that independent, not as freestanding as you would want a board to be?
SONNENFELD: Yes. They were cowardly. They collapsed to the imperial will of the president to intrude. Everybody knows that Donald Trump takes strong positions. He'll push and push to get whatever he wants. But they had no reason to not say no. If this was the Starlink board, let's say, where it's - perhaps 40%, 45% of the revenues come from government, you could say, well, there's a lot of influence there. And that's terrible. title: STAT+: In a rare move, the FDA cites two drugmakers for failing to report clinical trial results to a database
summary: For the first time in more than a year, the FDA sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
text:
For the first time in more than a year, the Food and Drug Administration has sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
The agency sends such notices when a trial sponsor fails to comply with a federal law that requires studies to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, a federal government database, within 21 days after the first human subject is enrolled. Summary results must also be posted to the database within 12 months after the trial’s primary completion date.
The FDA, however, has rarely sent noncompliance letters, despite years of criticism over lax enforcement. In recent years, calls for greater transparency have sparked a raft of studies showing a failure by drug companies, universities, and academic medical centers to comply with disclosure requirements. title: World Cup drove profits surge, says Marston's
summary: The company says an "excellent World Cup" helped drive strong trading as annual profits rose by 18%.
text:
World Cup drove profits surge, says Marston's
- Published
Pub company Marston's has said an "excellent World Cup" helped drive stronger trading as annual profits rose by nearly a fifth, despite reporting a dip in sales.
The Wolverhampton-based firm, which operates more than 1,300 pubs across the UK, reported underlying pre-tax profits of £85.4m for the year to 26 September, up 18.4% from a year earlier.
The company said trading was improved by new-look pubs, strong trade during this summer's football World Cup, and a partnership with Jeremy Clarkson's Hawkstone drinks brand.
"For the third year running, profit is significantly up, cash flow is strong and margins have improved," said chief executive Justin Platt.
The pub chain also said bookings for Christmas events were 9% ahead of the same point last year.
Marston's has invested heavily in refurbishing pubs into new formats, including its sports-focused "Grandstand" venues.
It plans at least 100 more conversions in the new financial year, in a bid to accelerate sales growth further.
One of the busiest locals during the World Cup was The New Spires in Coventry, which reopened in March following a £400,000 makeover.
The World Cup had been "very full on," said pub partner Pip Sullivan, explaining that on one match night alone they took more than £25,000 over the bar.
Marston's said it had selected the venue for investment because of its involvement with local sports teams, community groups, and charities.
"We've got two football teams, four darts teams and a dominoes team," explained Sullivan, all of which had also helped bolster sales.
But she recognised not all businesses were thriving.
"It's been a difficult year for a lot of pubs and we have empathised as they've lost a lot of trade," she said.
But investment by the company had brought the pub "back to life", she continued.
"We've managed to keep as much custom as we possibly can and seen new custom."
Marston's also pointed to events and promotions, including darts champion Luke Humphries' darts nights and the partnership with Clarkson.
"Guest satisfaction levels have improved again, thanks to the amazing work of our pub teams, whose passion and commitment keep our pubs at the heart of every local community they serve," added Platt.
"Our new pub formats are performing especially well and are now a proven growth engine for the business, giving us real confidence to accelerate our investment plans in 2027."

title: Opinion: Why medical students should keep going to class
summary: “Attending lectures in person has become … the most powerful way I take care of my mental health,” medical student Brian Zhang writes.
text:
This article is part of a new First Opinion series on the future of medical school.
By this time of year, the sky is black when I step outside. The day has carried me from lectures on gastrointestinal cancer disparities to TAing microbiology, from student government debates to helping free-clinic patients complete paperwork for expensive medications. With the cold nipping at my skin, I look back at the Stanford medical school building, its windows glowing. There is still so much to do, and even more to feel. I call my mother, my home base in human form. Three thousand miles away, she is preparing for bed. Circumstances beyond her control have kept her from taking a domestic flight for decades, let alone visit me in California. Her first question is always, “Did you remember to eat dinner?” Her second: “How were your classes today?”
I am a class-goer. Most of my classmates are, too, though preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic and the Step 1 exam’s transition to pass/fail. Given the flexibility of recordings and the time students devote to service, research, and other commitments, I understand why some choose to study independently and firmly believe in preserving students’ freedom to make that choice.
For me, though, attending lectures in person has become an important part of feeling at home. It is the most powerful way I take care of my mental health and the classmates I have come to see as my newfound family. I would like to make the case why it could for other medical students, too.
Part of that happiness comes from my daily calls with my immigrant mother. What I learn gives me something to share with the woman who gave up her dream of becoming a clinician so I could pursue mine: dissecting a cadaver for the first time, suturing, administering flu vaccines for undocumented folks, wrapping wound dressing around an unhoused man’s arm. Putting these experiences into words is an exercise of understanding the unmistakably human profession I am entering.
I once worried that telling her the good parts of my day would make the distance between us more painful. Her unconditional love for me throughout the years has taught me otherwise. There are many students like me who left the comfort of our communities to pursue higher education. We should not have to compromise on maintaining relationships with loved ones, which influences medical student well-being and belonging.
In graduate school, where life is more independent, class also gives us a place to come together. During lecture breaks, I learn about friends advocating against the medical bloodletting of horseshoe crabs, making spaces more accessible to people with disabilities, and bringing care to under-resourced youth through mobile vans. We ask to become involved in one another’s work. title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
text:
Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
- Published
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.
But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.
Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.
However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.
But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.
Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.
Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.
The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.
The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.
In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
